title: Social Dimensions of U.S. Trade Policies
abstract: The contributors to this volume include numerous members of the trade policy community who analyze and discuss the salient social dimensions of U.S. trade policies. These issues include the effects of trade on wage inequality; trade and immigration policy; U.S. trade adjustment assistance policies; the effects of NAFTA on environmental quality; the role of labor standards in U.S. trade policies; the economics of labor standards and the GATT; issues of child labor; and the role of interest groups in the design and implementation of U.S. trade policies. Chapter authors are Kyle Bagwell, Claude Barfield, George J. Borjas, Drusilla K. Brown, Alan V. Deardorff, Nancy Dunne, Gary S. Fields, John Kirton, Mike Jendrzejczyk, Phyllis Shearer Jones, Edward E. Leamer, Robert Naiman, Gregory K. Schoepfle, Robert W. Staiger, and Robert M. Stern. Commenters are Steve Beckman, Jagdish Bhagwati, Alan V. Deardorff, Avinash Dixit, Pharis Harvey, David van Hoogstraten, John H. Jackson, Lawrence Mishel, Jack Otero, J. David Richardson, Dani Rodrik, Mark Silbergeld, and T. N. Srinivasan. Alan V. Deardorff and Robert M. Stern are Professors of Economics and Public Policy, University of Michigan.

narrative:
Short impact summary

Social Dimensions of U.S. Trade Policies has accumulated 35 OpenAlex citations and sits in the top 10% of cited works for its field and year, indicating sustained scholarly uptake. Its citation record and topic profile show that the book has been used well beyond trade economics, especially in research on labor standards, wage inequality, immigration, and trade-policy politics, with clear policy relevance for decent work and economic growth.

Full narrative

Published by University of Michigan Press in 2000 as part of the Studies in International Economics series, Social Dimensions of U.S. Trade Policies brings together analysis of the social consequences of trade policy, including wage inequality, labor standards, child labor, immigration, adjustment assistance, and environmental effects. The book’s impact record shows a focused but durable scholarly afterlife: 35 OpenAlex citations place it in the top 10% of cited works for its field and publication year, a strong signal that the volume has remained useful to later researchers.

The citing literature is concentrated in economics and adjacent social-science fields, but it extends beyond a single discipline. Later work draws on the book in articles, book chapters, and preprints appearing in venues such as Journal of International Economics, Economica, Global Environmental Change, Regional Studies, and American Political Science Review. This pattern suggests that the book’s framing of trade as a social and political issue has continued to inform debates about labor markets, distribution, and governance.

The thematic spread of the citing record also points to cross-cutting relevance. Subsequent works connect to global trade and economics, gender and labor dynamics, poverty and child welfare, international development, and regional economic analysis. That range is consistent with a book that helped organize questions about who gains and who bears adjustment costs under trade liberalization, rather than one confined to a narrow trade-theory audience.

Beyond citation counts, the available record shows limited direct public-event or media evidence, so the strongest case for influence here is scholarly rather than broadcast. The book does, however, appear in library holdings and has an identifiable open instance in repository metadata, supporting discoverability. Overall, the evidence portrays a well-cited policy-oriented scholarly book whose influence lies in shaping later research on trade’s distributional and social consequences, particularly around labor, inequality, and decent work.
